processing: Base tea is mixed with fresh osmanthus so it absorbs the scent, then the flowers are sieved out and the tea is dried again; better grades are scented twice and finished with a light final scenting.
harvest_season: As with other osmanthus teas, the scenting follows the autumn bloom, using base tea made earlier in the year.
appearance_dry: Dark green twisted leaf, typically flecked with small golden-orange flowers.
appearance_liquor: Clear golden-yellow, as is typical of scented green tea.
appearance_wet: Soft green leaf with spent flowers among it.
taste_profile: Sweet osmanthus, often described as apricot-like in the flower, over a gentle green tea; a good one smells natural rather than sharp and is not noticeably bitter.

brewing.notes: Treat it like a green tea. Very hot water brings out the base leaf's bitterness and flattens the flower.

vintage_note: Usually sold undated or by the current scenting year, and best drunk within a year or so because the flower aroma fades.
description:
Osmanthus is the emblem flower of Guilin, whose name means osmanthus forest, so it makes sense that the city has its own scented tea. It is a tea and flower pairing more than a single defined leaf, usually sold on green tea, though black tea versions are made too.

The method is the classic one for flower teas: fresh blossoms and tea sit together, the leaf drinks in the aroma, the flowers are sifted out and the tea is dried again. The flowers you see in the bag may be added for looks, so they tell you little about how well it was scented.

A good cup smells of the flower first and tea second, soft and sweet, without anything stinging the nose. Brew it as you would a green tea, with water off the boil. Too hot and the base leaf takes over.

When buying, trust your nose over the colour of the blossoms. A perfumed smell that hits hard and vanishes after one steep suggests flavouring or weak scenting. Ask which base tea was used, since that decides the character of the cup.
history:
Little is documented about when Guilin's osmanthus tea began. The city's connection with the flower is old and well known, while the tea is best described as a local application of the general Chinese flower-scenting method.

Today it is common in Guilin, blended with green or black tea,.
